instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

listeningScripts.title: Gym Membership Cancellation
listeningScripts.text: Member: Hi, I'd like to cancel my gym membership. Customer Service Rep: I'd be happy to help. Can I ask why you're looking to cancel? Member: I'm relocating to British Columbia for work and won't be using the facility anymore. Rep: I understand. Let me pull up your account. What's your membership number? Member: It's GYM-47823. I've been a member for eighteen months. Rep: Great. I see you're on our premium monthly plan at $89 per month. When are you planning to move? Member: Three weeks from now. Rep: Okay. I can process the cancellation effective immediately, or we can set it to end on your move date. Which works better? Member: I prefer the move date, so three weeks from today. Rep: Perfect. That would be June 24th. I'll note that in your file. You won't be charged for July. However, I do need to let you know that you're in the middle of a two-year contract. There is a $150 early termination fee. Member: That's not fair. I wasn't told about that when I signed up. Rep: I apologize for that. Let me see what I can do. Since you've been loyal for eighteen months, I can reduce that fee to $75. That's the best I can offer. Member: Okay, I'll accept that.

listeningScripts.title: Roommate Household Discussion
listeningScripts.text: Alex: Hey, we need to talk about the dishes piling up in the sink. Jamie: Yeah, I know. I've been really busy with work this week. Alex: I get that, but it's been sitting there for three days. Jamie: I'm sorry, I'll do them tonight. Alex: Thanks. Also, we need to talk about the grocery situation. Jamie: What do you mean? Alex: I've been buying most of the groceries, and we're not splitting the cost fairly. Jamie: You're right. How do you want to handle it? Alex: We could split everything equally, or we could each buy our own stuff separately. Jamie: I think splitting equally makes more sense. We can keep a shared list. Alex: Great. One more thing—the internet bill is due next week. It's $75 this month. Jamie: That's higher than last month. Alex: Yeah, they increased the plan by five dollars. Jamie: Okay, so $37.50 each? Alex: Exactly. I'll send you a reminder.

listeningScripts.title: University Orientation: First Week Checklist
listeningScripts.text: Hello, welcome to orientation week. I'm here to walk you through essential tasks for your first week. First, attend your faculty's orientation meeting on Monday at ten AM in the Student Centre. Bring your student ID. Second, register for your courses online by Wednesday, August 28th. Early registration means better class times. Third, purchase your textbooks from the university bookstore before classes start. Fourth, get your student photo ID taken at the Services Office between 9 and 4 on any day this week. The photo ID is required for library access and residence entry. Fifth, activate your email account at the IT support desk. Your email is your primary communication channel for all university announcements. Sixth, find your classes on a campus map. Most buildings are located around the central quad. Seventh, attend the Welcome Social on Friday evening in the gymnasium. It's a great way to meet other students and faculty. Eighth, complete your health and immunization form at Student Health Services. This is mandatory before attending classes. Finally, budget about three hundred dollars for books and materials. Questions? Visit the information desk in the main foyer.

listeningScripts.title: Alberta Heritage Museum Expansion
listeningScripts.text: The Alberta Heritage Museum is embarking on a 95 million dollar expansion project that will double its exhibition space. The project, spanning five years, will create new galleries dedicated to Indigenous history, early settlement, and contemporary Alberta culture. Museum Director Patricia Wong announced that the expansion will feature interactive exhibits and state-of-the-art multimedia installations. The project will generate approximately 600 construction jobs over the expansion period. Funding comes from government grants, private donations, and corporate sponsorships. The museum currently attracts 480,000 visitors annually, and officials project this will increase by 45 percent following the expansion. A new 2,000-square-meter research and conservation facility will support artifact preservation. Four new galleries will be built, including a dedicated space for rotating temporary exhibitions. Community consultation has identified strong public support, with 78 percent of surveyed Albertans favoring the project. The expansion is scheduled to be completed by 2031.

listeningScripts.title: University Program Expansion Planning
listeningScripts.text:
Dean Robert: We've been asked to consider expanding our engineering program, particularly in renewable energy studies. The faculty has requested three additional full-time instructors and funding for new laboratory equipment. The cost would be approximately 2.4 million dollars over two years. Given our current budget constraints, I'm hesitant to commit to this expansion.

Professor Elena: I understand the budget concerns, Dean, but we're actually losing enrollment to competing universities who offer these programs. Last year, we lost 150 potential engineering students to schools with stronger renewable energy options. If we don't expand now, we'll fall behind. Plus, there's significant industry demand for graduates with renewable energy expertise. Companies are specifically recruiting from universities with these specialized programs.

Student Representative Malik: From a student perspective, I absolutely support this expansion. Many of my classmates are interested in sustainability and green technology, but we don't have the courses or facilities to support that focus. I think this investment would make our university much more attractive to prospective students, which would actually increase our overall enrollment and revenue.

Budget Committee Member Diana: Malik makes a good point about revenue. If this program attracts even 200 additional students, the tuition revenue would exceed the expansion costs within three years. And we could explore partnerships with industry for funding. I've been in conversations with several renewable energy companies that might contribute equipment or funding in exchange for access to our graduates for recruitment.

listeningScripts.title: Climate Migration and Urban Planning
listeningScripts.text: Climate change is already forcing large-scale human migration, and we need to prepare for it now. Rising sea levels, extreme weather, and changing precipitation patterns are making entire regions uninhabitable. We're not just talking about future problems—this is happening today. Small island nations are literally disappearing. Coastal cities are experiencing increased flooding. Agricultural regions are becoming deserts. Where will these people go? History shows us that unplanned migration creates chaos: overcrowded cities, slums, resource conflicts, and instability. I believe cities and countries need to proactively plan for climate migration. This means developing infrastructure and housing in climate-resilient areas, creating economic opportunities for migrants, and managing population flows thoughtfully. Canada and the northern regions of other countries will likely become more desirable as climate conditions shift. Rather than letting this happen chaotically, we should be designing inclusive urban expansion, building climate-resilient communities, and preparing labor markets for population shifts. Some people see climate migration as a negative, but it's inevitable. The real question is whether we manage it responsibly or let it cause humanitarian crises. I'm advocating for proactive planning now. We should be expanding housing, infrastructure, and economic capacity in climate-safe regions. We should also help other countries adapt in place where possible. But denying this reality and refusing to plan is irresponsible.
